newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's future leader Tung yet to doff business hat.
newsitem.headline: HK's future leader Tung yet to doff business hat.

text.p: There is a big difference between being chairman of a corporation and the head of Hong Kong -- and political analysts say Tung Chee-hwa has not quite made the transition yet.
"He hasn't really been able to put away his hat as the businessman yet," analyst and columnist Andy Ho told Reuters.
"His way of doing things is still very much that of the boss of a corporation rather than a leader, a political leader. He has not been taking public opinion very seriously."

Tung stepped from the helm of his family's shipping empire into the glare of the political spotlight when a Beijing-backed committee picked him to run Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.

Although opinion polls show Tung enjoys the backing of a majority of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people, questions linger about his independence from China's top bosses and his ability to deal with the territory's bread-and-butter issues.

While he was quick to step down as chairman of Orient Overseas (International) Ltd ahead of his campaign for post-handover Chief Executive, he has been much slower to shed his businessman image, analysts said.

"Here we have a person who has not been a politician as such -- who has been very much in the business sector -- who has now been invested with power," Hong Kong University law professor Nihal Jayawickrama told Reuters.
"At some point in time he'll have to make a clean break. Perhaps he feels that should be done on the first of July, but I think this sort of situation could go on recurring."
Tung caused a flap last week when he appointed property surveyor and real estate consultant Leung Chun-ying to head a committee mapping out housing strategy in the territory.
With property prices booming and the government waging a deliberate but delicate campaign against speculators, housing is a highly sensitive issue.
Critics saw the appointment as ripe for a conflict of interest, and ordinary citizens expressed their dissatisfaction on radio talk shows and in letters to newspapers.
An opinion poll published on March 25 by the independent Ming Pao newspaper showed Tung's scores for ability and credibility had dropped since a similar survey a month earlier.
It attributed the decline to Tung's appointment of Leung.

Tung also came under fire last week for mixing business and politics when he told an audience in his birth town of Shanghai that Shanghai Industrial Holdings Ltd had been "a good performer for H-shares" on Hong Kong's stock exchange.
H-shares are China-incorporated firms listed in Hong Kong, although Shanghai Industrial is in fact not an H-share but a red chip -- a Hong Kong-incorporated firm with strong China ties.
Legislators and newspaper columnists were quick to point out that Tung should not have singled out a company for praise, no matter how successful it has been.

A South China Morning Post columnist said a stockbroker contact of his was not sure which was the greatest cause for concern -- that Tung was recommending stocks, that he didn't know the difference between an H-share and a red chip, or that Shanghai Industrial shares fell the day after his endorsement.

Tung has been criticised for being too much a Beijing man and too much a businessman, Ho said, but added that "on the whole, he has performed quite well" in his first 100 days as Chief Executive-designate.

Ho said Tung's first true test would come when he assumes office on July 1 and must oversee the setting up a new electoral system and the establishment of new laws as well as follow up on promises he has made on housing and education.
"During the campaign he was very available, he was available to everybody," Ho said. "But once he was elected he seems to be formulating plans, making decisions, mostly on his own."
